terms.definition: An element with properties between those of metals and nonmetals.
terms.function: Fills the in-between zone of the periodic table and behaves part-way between the two great families.
terms.whereItIs: Along the diagonal staircase of the periodic table.
terms.whyItMatters: Metalloids like silicon are the foundation of modern electronics.

terms.definition: The zigzag diagonal line on the periodic table that separates the metals from the nonmetals.
terms.function: Marks where the metalloids sit — the elements that border both families.
terms.whereItIs: The glowing diagonal of tiles across the table section in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: The staircase is the table's physical dividing line, and the metalloids live right on it.

terms.definition: A material that conducts electricity part-way — better than an insulator, worse than a metal — and can be switched.
terms.function: Lets electronic devices control electric current precisely, which is how chips compute.
terms.whereItIs: The half-filled meter beside the wafer in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Semiconduction is why metalloids like silicon power phones, computers, and solar cells.

terms.definition: The most famous metalloid, sitting on the staircase at Group 14; the raw material of computer chips.
terms.function: Acts as the semiconductor inside virtually all modern electronic devices.
terms.whereItIs: The round wafer at the center of the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Silicon's switchable conduction built the digital age.
